evidence: Vitruvius 5.11.2: exhedrae spatiōsae, habentēs sēdēs (so spelt in the Latin Library text)
terms.comment: Classically a room furnished with seats, for conversation; in Cicero the room where the speakers of a dialogue sit and talk. Traupman gives it for “sitting room”. The e is short (Greek ἐξέδρα). Use it for the room’s function; summum tabulātum describes its position in the house.

evidence: Dig. 9.3.5.2: ex mediānō cēnāculī (Lewis & Short, s.v. mediānus)
terms.comment: In the Digest the middle part of an upper flat, not a named room; Andresian’s word for the living room. exedra is classical.

phrases.latin: Culīnam habet, cubicula, inter quae hospitium est, balneum, lātrīnam, hortum, trīclīnium, exedram
phrases.english: It has a kitchen, bedrooms (among them a guest room), a bathroom, a lavatory, a garden, a dining room and a sitting room
phrases.source: Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam

sessorium.html: Traupman (pp. 124–125) gives sessōrium for “living room”, but its ancient senses are “seat, stool” (Caelius Aurelianus) and, in a single passage, “dwelling” (Petronius 77.4 vīperae hujus sessōrium) (Lewis & Short).

sources: Lewis & Short: exedra · Lewis & Short: sessorium
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 124–125.
